screens.title: Contract Security Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Designing Ethereum contracts to prevent fund loss and logic exploits

narration.text: Smart contract security is the difference between a resilient service and irreversible loss. In this chapter you will learn how common vulnerabilities work, why they matter, and how to defend your contracts in production. We begin with reentrancy — an attacker pattern that repeatedly re-enters a function to drain funds — then apply the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern and optional reentrancy guards as practical defenses. You will review integer overflow and underflow concepts and why Solidity 0.8 stops many of those issues by default. We also cover access control: the simple onlyOwner modifier and the more flexible Role-Based Access Control pattern. Finally, you will study front-running and denial-of-service vectors and how testing, audits, and bug bounties reduce risk. A short live-coding task at the end walks you through refactoring a vulnerable withdraw pattern into a secure implementation. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to spot vulnerable code patterns, apply defensive coding rules, and choose appropriate access controls. Think about a contract you maintain — what single change could reduce its attack surface right away?

keyIdea.title: Why security-first matters
keyIdea.text: Smart contract bugs can cause permanent financial loss. Build contracts with defensive patterns, clear access control, and rigorous testing from day one.

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will identify common vulnerabilities, apply defensive patterns, and choose appropriate access controls. First, you will learn to recognize reentrancy and how a malicious external call can re-enter your contract before its state is updated, with a concrete withdrawal example you can reproduce in a test. Second, you will implement Checks-Effects-Interactions and an explicit reentrancy guard pattern so that state updates always precede external transfers. Third, you will understand integer overflow and underflow history and why modern Solidity reverts arithmetic out-of-bounds by default, plus when SafeMath is still relevant for legacy code. Fourth, you will design and reason about access control, from a single owner to role-based systems. Each objective includes a practical milestone you can verify with unit tests. These skills help prevent catastrophic losses and make your contracts auditable and maintainable. Which objective would give the biggest immediate risk reduction for the contracts you manage?

screens.title: Reentrancy — What it is and why it matters
screens.subtitle: How external calls can allow repeated execution and fund draining

narration.text: Reentrancy is a bug class where a contract calls an external address and that call causes execution to re-enter the original contract before its internal state is updated. Concretely, imagine a withdraw function that sends Ether and then sets the caller balance to zero. If a malicious contract receives Ether and immediately calls withdraw again, it finds the old balance still present and can drain funds multiple times. That simple example shows why order matters: external interactions must never occur before finalizing the contract's internal state for that operation. A common misconception is that only complex contracts face reentrancy; in reality any function that sends Ether or makes external calls may be vulnerable. A concrete test example is deploying a simple attacker contract which in its fallback calls withdraw repeatedly; running this scenario demonstrates the vulnerability and the attacker's profits. The key takeaway is a defensive posture: assume external calls can do anything, perform checks first, update state next, and then interact externally, or use a guard to prevent re-entrance. Ask yourself: does any external call in your contract happen before a state change it depends on?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Reentrancy happens when external calls re-enter a contract before state updates, allowing repeated, unintended execution.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Reentrancy — What it is and why it matters
Definition & core idea
An external call can re-enter your contract and run logic that assumes earlier state changes have occurred. This can lead to repeated withdrawals or inconsistent state.
Misconception: Only complex contracts are vulnerable. Small withdraw patterns are at risk too.
Concrete scenario: A malicious contract receives Ether and its fallback function calls withdraw repeatedly to drain the balance.
Why it matters: Funds can be drained irreversibly on-chain; tests must reproduce the attack path.
Key Takeaway

Assume external calls may call back into your contract; design state updates so that a reentrant call cannot observe stale state.

Analogy & guided test
Analogy: think of handing a key to a stranger mid-transaction. If you then change the lock after they act, the sequence allowed them extra access. Guided test: deploy a simple vulnerable withdraw contract and an attacker contract that calls withdraw from its fallback. Observe the victim contract balance fall faster than expected.
Check your understanding
  • What function orders allow reentrancy?
  • How could a fallback function be used to re-enter?
  • Which tests would reproduce the attack?

screens.title: Vulnerable withdraw example
screens.subtitle: Read and reason about a withdrawal pattern that allows reentrancy

narration.text: We'll walk through a classic vulnerable withdraw implementation to see where the flaw appears and how an attacker exploits it. The vulnerable pattern reads the user's balance, sends Ether to the caller using a low-level call, then sets the balance to zero. The critical mistake is performing the external call before the state update. In a test, an attacker contract receives Ether and, in its fallback callback, calls withdraw again. Because the original balance is unchanged until after the external call, the attacker can withdraw repeatedly in the same transaction. A common misconception is that higher-level transfer functions always protect you; low-level calls like call forward gas and permit re-entry. To validate this in a local environment, deploy the vulnerable contract, fund it, then deploy an attacker which triggers the fallback re-entry. Observe the victim contract balance drop unexpectedly. The model takeaway is simple: when you see external calls inside a stateful function, treat them as invasive operations that can be exploited. Later we'll refactor the same code to a secure version using Checks-Effects-Interactions and a no-reentrancy guard. Vulnerable withdraw example means external call before state update allows a reentrant caller to repeatedly observe and withdraw a non-zero balance.. In practical terms, read and reason about a withdrawal pattern that allows reentrancy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Vulnerability pattern
keyIdea.text: External call before state update allows a reentrant caller to repeatedly observe and withdraw a non-zero balance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Vulnerable withdraw example
Vulnerable contract (read-only)
// VulnerableWithdraw
contract VulnerableWithdraw {
  mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

  function deposit() public payable {
    balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
  }

  function withdraw() public {
    uint256 amount = balances[msg.sender];
    require(amount > 0, "No funds to withdraw");

    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}(""); // External call BEFORE state update
    require(success, "Transfer failed");

    balances[msg.sender] = 0; // State update AFTER external call
  }
}
Note how the external call precedes the state change. The attacker’s fallback will re-enter before balances[msg.sender] is cleared.
Exploit scenario and tests
Deploy this contract and an attacker that calls withdraw from its fallback. In a unit test, fund the victim, call deposit from the attacker, then trigger withdraw. The victim’s balance will fall by more than the attacker’s deposit if reentrancy succeeds.
Common mistake: Assuming transfer/revert will block reentrancy. Low-level call forwards gas; never rely on it for safety.
Key Takeaway

Always update balances and critical state before making external calls. Validate by writing a test that simulates a reentrant caller.

screens.title: Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern
screens.subtitle: A three-step defensive pattern to prevent reentrancy

narration.text: The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern offers a simple rule: first perform all checks, then apply effects to state, and only after that perform external interactions. Checks are require statements and guard conditions that validate inputs and permissions. Effects are deterministic changes to your contract’s state like subtracting balances or updating status flags. Interactions are any external calls, including sending Ether or calling other contracts. The practical reason this works is that by the time external code runs, the contract’s state reflects the completed operation, so a reentrant call can no longer observe stale data to repeat the operation. A common misconception is that this pattern alone is always sufficient; while it prevents many reentrancy cases, combining it with a reentrancy guard provides defence-in-depth. For example, a withdraw function should require a positive balance, set the balance to zero, then perform the transfer. In unit tests, assert that a reentrant attacker cannot increase withdrawals. The pattern is easy to read and should be enforced as a code-base standard: checks first, effects second, interactions last. Which function in your code violates this order right now?

keyIdea.title: 3-step rule
keyIdea.text: Checks first, Effects (state updates) second, Interactions (external calls) last — reduces window for reentrancy.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern
Pattern steps
Checks — validate input, require balance > 0, confirm permissions.
Effects — update state: subtract or zero balances, set flags.
Interactions — make external calls or transfers only after state is final.
Adopt this ordering in code reviews and automate checks with linters or pre-commit policies. When combined with guards, it becomes a reliable defense pattern.
Example refactor
// Before: external call before state update
// After: checks, effects, then interactions (transfer)
function withdraw() public {
  uint256 amount = balances[msg.sender];
  require(amount > 0, "No funds"); // CHECK

  balances[msg.sender] = 0; // EFFECT

  (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}(""); // INTERACTION
  require(success, "Transfer failed");
}
Pro-tip: Combine with a reentrancy guard for defense-in-depth.
Common mistake: Side-effects that depend on external call return values can reintroduce vulnerabilities.

screens.title: Reentrancy Guard and secure withdraw
screens.subtitle: Apply a simple mutex and put state updates before interactions

narration.text: A reentrancy guard is a mutex-like pattern that prevents a function from being entered while it is already running. It is often implemented with a boolean locked flag and a modifier that sets the flag true before execution and false after. In practice, you apply this modifier to state-changing functions that perform external calls. Combined with Checks-Effects-Interactions, the guard provides a second line of defense: even if an ordering mistake slips through, the guard blocks nested calls. The secure withdraw pattern sets the balance to zero, uses a no-reentrancy modifier, then transfers Ether. A common misconception is that a guard replaces the need for correct state ordering — it does not; use both. In unit tests, apply the same attacker contract used earlier: with the guard in place, reentrancy attempts should revert at the modifier check. This pattern is widely adopted and implemented in audited libraries, but understanding the underlying boolean lock helps when auditing or debugging third-party code. The real insight is to treat the guard and proper ordering as complementary safeguards. Reentrancy Guard and secure withdraw means a mutex-like modifier blocks nested calls and complements checks-effects-interactions for robust protection.. In practical terms, apply a simple mutex and put state updates before interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reentrancy guard
keyIdea.text: A mutex-like modifier blocks nested calls and complements Checks-Effects-Interactions for robust protection.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Reentrancy Guard and secure withdraw
Secure contract example
contract SecureWithdraw {
  mapping(address => uint256) public balances;
  bool private locked; // simple reentrancy guard

  modifier noReentrancy() {
    require(!locked, "Reentrant call detected");
    locked = true;
    _;
    locked = false;
  }

  function deposit() public payable {
    balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
  }

  function withdraw() public noReentrancy {
    uint256 amount = balances[msg.sender];
    require(amount > 0, "No funds to withdraw");

    balances[msg.sender] = 0; // EFFECT

    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}(""); // INTERACTION
    require(success, "Transfer failed");
  }
}
This example shows the guard modifier and the Effects-before-Interactions ordering together.
Why both measures matter
The guard blocks nested entries into the function body, while ordering ensures state is consistent if an interaction occurs. Defense-in-depth reduces the chance a single missed check produces a catastrophic exploit.
Pro-tip: Use audited library implementations for production, but review logic to ensure the ordering is correct.
Common mistake: Forgetting to reset the locked flag on early returns or reverts can lock out functionality; prefer well-tested patterns.

screens.title: Integer overflow and underflow
screens.subtitle: What arithmetic wrapping means and modern mitigations

narration.text: Integer overflow happens when a value exceeds the maximum representable number for its type and wraps around to a low value; underflow is the reverse. Historically, unsigned integer wrap-around allowed attackers to increase balances by exploiting arithmetic that wrapped to a large number. Modern Solidity compilers starting at version 0.8.0 automatically revert transactions when arithmetic would overflow or underflow, which mitigates most accidental wrap issues. However, legacy contracts or operations in inline assembly may still be vulnerable. For older codebases, libraries like SafeMath were used to check arithmetic before operating. A common misconception is that compiler defaults always protect you — while recent compilers help, reading third-party code and any assembly paths is essential. When unit testing, include boundary tests for maximum and minimum values and fuzz tests that feed unexpected large numbers. If your contract must interoperate with older contracts, audit those interaction points carefully for arithmetic assumptions. The takeaway is to prefer modern compiler defaults and add explicit checks around critical arithmetic when necessary. Integer overflow and underflow means solidity 0.8+ reverts on overflow/underflow; legacy code required safemath or manual checks.. In practical terms, what arithmetic wrapping means and modern mitigations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Arithmetic safety
keyIdea.text: Solidity 0.8+ reverts on overflow/underflow; legacy code required SafeMath or manual checks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Integer overflow and underflow
What happens
Overflow: value exceeds type max and wraps; underflow: goes below zero and wraps. Attacks previously used wrapping to manipulate balances.
Mitigation: Solidity 0.8+ reverts on overflow/underflow by default. For legacy code, use SafeMath.
Key Takeaway

Prefer modern compilers and add focused boundary tests. When interacting with old contracts, inspect arithmetic carefully.

Testing & examples
Add unit tests that send maximum values and near-zero values into functions that perform arithmetic. Use fuzzing to discover unexpected inputs. If your code uses assembly, add extra scrutiny because compiler protections may not apply.
Example test: deposit a near-max uint256 and attempt to add an amount that would overflow — expect a revert under Solidity 0.8+.
Common mistake: Assuming external library calls always return checked values; always validate results you depend on.

screens.title: Access control: onlyOwner and RBAC
screens.subtitle: Simple ownership vs flexible role-based permissions

narration.text: Access control restricts who can call sensitive functions. The simplest pattern is onlyOwner: store an owner address in the constructor and gate functions with a modifier that requires the caller match that address. This is easy to understand and suitable for small projects, but it centralizes power and lacks delegation. Role-Based Access Control, by contrast, assigns named roles to addresses and checks roles at runtime. RBAC gives you fine-grained permissions, so you can grant a minter role to a separate service without giving it full owner privileges. A common misconception is that RBAC is always more secure; it is more flexible but adds complexity and more potential misconfigurations. Use audited implementations like OpenZeppelin’s AccessControl and ensure role management functions are themselves protected and auditable. In tests, assert that only authorized accounts perform actions and that role changes behave as intended. For production systems, combine RBAC with multisig or timelock patterns to reduce single-point failures. Which model fits your governance and upgrade needs? Access control: onlyOwner and RBAC means onlyowner is simple; rbac is flexible but requires careful management and testing of role assignments.. In practical terms, simple ownership vs flexible role-based permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Access control choices
keyIdea.text: onlyOwner is simple; RBAC is flexible but requires careful management and testing of role assignments.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Access control: onlyOwner and RBAC
onlyOwner pattern
contract AdminControlled {
  address public owner;
  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
  modifier onlyOwner() {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Not authorized");
    _;
  }
  function sensitiveFunction() public onlyOwner { /* ... */ }
}
Use onlyOwner for small teams but plan for recovery and ownership transfer controls.
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
RBAC defines named roles like MINTER_ROLE and PAUSER_ROLE and assigns them to addresses. Functions check whether the caller has the required role. This allows granular delegation without exposing full owner privileges. Prefer audited libraries and test role grants and revocations.
Pro-tip: Protect role-granting functions with multisig or timelock for high value systems.
Common mistake: Over-granting roles or leaving a role open to any caller; always require authorization for role changes.

narration.text: Comparing onlyOwner and RBAC helps you choose the right model: onlyOwner stores a single authoritative address and is easy to reason about and test; RBAC defines roles and allows multiple addresses to hold specialized permissions. OnlyOwner is lower complexity and less error-prone for very small projects, but it centralizes power and creates a single point of failure. RBAC reduces the need to share private keys by assigning roles to services, multisigs, or governance contracts, but it increases configuration surface and the need to secure role-management functions. A misconception is that RBAC eliminates the need for governance — it does not; role assignment and revocation must themselves be guarded, often with multisig or timelocks. In unit tests, cover both allowed and disallowed callers for each function and include scenarios where roles are transferred or revoked to ensure no privilege escalation paths exist. Choose the approach that aligns with your operational model and risk tolerance, and always prefer audited, community-trusted implementations for production. onlyOwner vs Role-Based Access Control means onlyowner is simple and auditable; rbac scales delegation but requires careful role governance and testing.. In practical terms, trade-offs between simplicity and flexibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-offs
keyIdea.text: onlyOwner is simple and auditable; RBAC scales delegation but requires careful role governance and testing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › onlyOwner vs Role-Based Access Control
onlyOwner
  • Single owner address controls sensitive functions.
  • Easy to implement and audit.
  • Risk: single point of compromise.
RBAC
  • Named roles for fine-grained permissions.
  • Supports delegation without sharing keys.
  • Requires secure role management and tests for role changes.
Use RBAC when roles map to different services or teams.
Use onlyOwner for small single-admin deployments with clear recovery plans.
Always test revoked role scenarios and the role-granting pathways.

screens.title: Front-running
screens.subtitle: How transaction ordering can be abused and mitigations

narration.text: Front-running occurs when an attacker sees a pending transaction and submits their own with a higher gas price to get included earlier in the block. On DEXs or auctions this can let the attacker obtain a favorable trade or bid before the original transaction executes. Defenses include commit-reveal schemes where users first commit a hash and reveal later, making the content of the operation unavailable to observers until it is committed. Another approach is to design contract APIs that reduce the value of ordering advantages, or use off-chain coordination and on-chain settlement primitives that batch operations. A common misconception is that private mempools eliminate front-running; private relays reduce exposure but do not remove systemic ordering risk. In testing, mimic an attacker that re-submits the same transaction with higher fees and confirm your mitigation makes the attack unprofitable or impossible. For critical applications, consider designing economic disincentives or time locks so that the cost of front-running outweighs potential gains. Which user flows in your contract expose high-value ordering risk? Front-running means use commit-reveal, batching, or economic disincentives to reduce the value of seeing and re-ordering pending transactions.. In practical terms, how transaction ordering can be abused and mitigations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Front-running defense
keyIdea.text: Use commit-reveal, batching, or economic disincentives to reduce the value of seeing and re-ordering pending transactions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Front-running
How it works
An attacker watches the mempool and races to submit a transaction with higher gas to get executed earlier, profiting from ordering advantages.
Mitigations: commit-reveal, batching, economic disincentives, and minimizing high-value single transactions.
Testing and example
Simulate an attacker by re-submitting a transaction with higher gas price in a test environment. Verify the commit-reveal flow prevents the attacker from learning the revealed value before commit finalization.
Analogy: sealed-bid auction prevents bidders from reacting to visible bids; commit-reveal is the sealed bid equivalent on-chain.
Common misassumption: Private mempools replace protocol-level mitigations; they reduce exposure but are not a full solution.

screens.title: Denial of Service (DoS)
screens.subtitle: Preventing operations that can be blocked or exhausted

narration.text: Denial of service in smart contracts can take several forms: making a function revert for everyone, exhausting gas through unbounded loops, or breaking payment loops by sending Ether to a contract that deliberately reverts. A common dangerous pattern is iterating over a dynamically growing array and performing external calls for each element. If an attacker fills the array or a particular recipient reverts, the entire function can fail for honest users. Defenses include avoiding unbounded loops, using pull-payment models where recipients withdraw funds rather than being pushed to, and isolating external interactions so one bad recipient does not halt others. Another mitigation is graceful failure handling: instead of reverting the entire function, record failures and allow manual retry or refunds. Testing should include scenarios where recipients reject transfers and where large amounts of data are processed. Always assume external recipients may behave maliciously and design for failure paths that preserve contract liveness. Which push payments in your code could be changed to pull payments today? Denial of Service (DoS) means avoid unbounded loops and push payments; prefer pull patterns and handle external call failures gracefully to maintain liveness.. In practical terms, preventing operations that can be blocked or exhausted. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DoS avoidance
keyIdea.text: Avoid unbounded loops and push payments; prefer pull patterns and handle external call failures gracefully to maintain liveness.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Denial of Service (DoS)
Common DoS patterns
  • Unbounded loops over growing arrays.
  • Push payments that revert because a recipient is hostile.
  • Functions that rely on external calls to succeed for all cases.
Mitigations and tests
Prefer pull payments so recipients call withdraw. Limit per-transaction processing and paginate work. Add tests where recipients revert or gas is exhausted, and ensure the contract remains usable for honest users.
Pro-tip: Use events to record failed operations and allow off-chain operators to remediate.
Common mistake: Assuming all recipients are well-behaved; always code for failure.

screens.title: Security-first mindset: testing, audits, and bounties
screens.subtitle: A practical process to reduce risk from development through deployment

narration.text: A security-first mindset treats security as an integral part of design and delivery rather than an afterthought. Start with unit tests that cover expected and edge cases, add integration tests that exercise interactions between contracts, and use fuzz testing to explore unexpected inputs. For critical code paths, write reproducible exploit tests that show the vulnerability and confirm the fix. Formal verification is appropriate for very high value contracts where mathematical proofs are feasible. Before production deploys, engage external auditors to review code and threat models, and follow up with a public bug bounty program to leverage community reviews. A common misconception is that tests alone are sufficient; they reduce risk but do not replace an independent audit. When you fix issues, include the exploit test in your suite so regressions are visible. Also keep dependencies and compiler versions up-to-date so you benefit from security improvements such as automatic overflow checks. The result is a repeatable safety pipeline: tests, audits, fixes with exploit tests, and a live bounty program — all minimizing risk before and after deployment. Security-first mindset: testing, audits, and bounties means combine tests, fuzzing, audits, verification, and bounties to create a repeatable risk-reduction process before deployment.. In practical terms, a practical process to reduce risk from development through deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Security pipeline
keyIdea.text: Combine tests, fuzzing, audits, verification, and bounties to create a repeatable risk-reduction process before deployment.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Security-first mindset: testing, audits, and bounties
Repeatable pipeline
1. Unit tests including edge cases and exploit reproduction tests.
2. Integration tests and fuzzing to explore unexpected inputs.
3. External audits and formal verification where appropriate.
4. Bug bounty programs to catch issues in production scenarios.
When an audit finds an issue, add a test that reproduces the exploit and include it in CI so fixes remain validated. Track compiler and dependency updates as part of maintenance to inherit security improvements.
Concrete activity
As a hands-on task, refactor a vulnerable withdraw to secure form, write an exploit test that fails on the vulnerable code, then show the test passes after the fix. This confirms both the vulnerability and the remediation.
Key Takeaway

Security is a continuous process: tests, audits, and bounties keep contracts safer over time. Make exploit tests part of your codebase.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Core ideas to keep top of mind

narration.text: Here are essential concepts to retain: Reentrancy occurs when an external call allows repeated entry into a function before state updates. The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern prevents this by validating inputs, updating state, then performing external interactions. A reentrancy guard provides an additional mutex to block nested calls. Integer overflow and underflow used to be a practical attack vector; modern Solidity reverts arithmetic exceptions by default, but legacy code or assembly paths require careful review. Keep these concepts in mind as invariants when you audit or refactor code, and always write tests to demonstrate both the exploit and the fix. These short reminders will help you quickly recognize risky patterns during code review. Which of these concepts did you find easiest to apply in your current contracts? content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts — Part 1
Reentrancy
External calls can re-enter the contract and exploit unchanged state.
Checks-Effects-Interactions
Perform validations, update state, then make external interactions.
Reentrancy Guard
A mutex-like modifier that prevents nested calls into a protected function.
Summary: Use CEI and guards together, test exploit scenarios, and keep compiler and library versions current to reduce risk.

narration.text: Remember these complementary concepts: integer overflow and underflow risks are largely mitigated by modern Solidity, but legacy code and assembly require vigilance. Access control choices matter — onlyOwner is simple, RBAC scales delegation but needs secure role management. Front-running and DoS are real economic and availability risks; mitigate them with commit-reveal, batching, pull-payments, and limiting per-transaction work. Finally, a security-first workflow of unit tests, fuzzing, audits, formal verification when needed, and bug bounties is how teams reduce risk over time. Embed exploit tests as regression guards so fixes remain validated. These practices, when combined, form a layered defense that reduces the chance of catastrophic loss. keyIdea.title: Complementary practices
keyIdea.text: Combine arithmetic safety, access control, front-running/DoS mitigations, and a security pipeline to reduce systemic risk.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts — Part 2
Integer safety
Prefer Solidity 0.8+ which reverts on overflow; audit legacy arithmetic and assembly paths.
Front-running & DoS
Use commit-reveal and pull patterns; avoid unbounded iterations and fragile external dependencies.
Testing & audits
Make exploit tests part of CI, perform audits, and run bug bounties to catch post-deployment issues.
Final takeaway: layered defenses and rigorous verification reduce the probability and impact of security incidents. Make the practices routine.

ai_generation_note: Create a 15-minute live coding demonstration in Remix. Start by deploying a `VulnerableEtherStore` contract. Show a step-by-step attack using a simple `Attacker` contract to demonstrate reentrancy, visually tracking the contract's balance in the Remix console. Then, refactor the `VulnerableEtherStore` into `SecureEtherStore` by applying the `noReentrancy` modifier and the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. Re-run the attack to show it fails. Include visual overlays explaining each step of the attack and mitigation. End with a safety note emphasizing the importance of audits.
